subject: rakali water rat
title: Australian Water Rats Rip the Hearts Out of Poisonous Toads

scenes.text: Cane toads are covered in poison. This rat eats their hearts.
In 2014, scientists in Western Australia found up to five freshly killed toads every morning.
Each one was opened up, the heart and liver gone.
On smaller toads, the killer peeled the toxic skin off the back legs and ate the meat.
It was the rakali, Australia's native water rat, and it leaves the poison glands behind.
Toads reached that creek less than two years earlier. The rats had already cracked them.

description:
Cane toads are covered in poison, yet Australia's native water rat eats their hearts.
In 2014, at a creek in the Kimberley, Western Australia, researchers found up to five freshly killed cane toads each morning. Large toads had their heart and liver removed and the gall bladder pulled out of the chest; on medium toads the rats also stripped the toxic skin off the back legs and ate the meat. The toad's toxin is made in parotoid glands on its back, neck and shoulders. The rakali (Hydromys chrysogaster), which can grow to over 1 kg, preferred the largest toads, and was doing this less than two years after toads arrived in 2011-12 (Parrott and Clulow, Australian Mammalogy, 2019).
Which animal do you think has the cleverest way to eat something dangerous?
first_comment: Bonus fact: the rats ignored small toads and went for the biggest ones, even though medium toads outnumbered large ones 27 to 1. Why go big?
